title: A Framework To Assess The Transformative Potential Of Transdisciplinary Research: Application To Cases In The European Alps
abstract: The implementation of transformative changes that address the root causes of social–ecological challenges is urgently needed. Transdisciplinary research has been proposed as one suitable approach to coproduce relevant knowledge for transformative change. However, there is a lack of conceptual clarity to assess whether and how transdisciplinary research can deliver transformative change, and also about what transformative change is. Here, we present a framework to assess the transformative potential of transdisciplinary research and test it in 4 cases from the European Alps. The framework includes a characterization of the transdisciplinary research process, a characterization of the changes in the target unit (the entity that the transdisciplinary research aims to transform), and a theory of change linking the former to the latter. The framework allows examination of whether and how transdisciplinary research contributes to changing target units and to what extent these changes are transformative, while highlighting the importance of the temporal context. In addition, the framework highlights key characteristics of the transdisciplinary research process that shape its transformative potential. The main value of the framework lies in the explicit link between the assessment of the transdisciplinary research process and the assessment of transformative change over the medium term (from years to decades). Moving forward, studies are needed that rely on a larger and more diverse number of cases and that better grasp the depth of transformative change. This article offers insights for improving assessments of the impacts of research, which are increasingly critical for researchers, universities, funders, and beneficiaries. These insights can support the effective design and evaluation of research aimed at implementing transformative change to address complex social–ecological challenges.

title: When bots act like us: the role of social media accounts' human-likeness in opinion polarization
abstract: Purpose As social bots penetrate social media, social media accounts with different human-likeness interact with each other, with opinion polarization as one of the results. This study investigates the impact of human-likeness of social media accounts on opinion polarization on social media. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the social validation principle and its intersections with the optimal distinctiveness theory as the theoretical foundation, this study applies empirical analysis with a dataset of 2,034,201 replies from Weibo to examine the proposed model. Findings An inverted U-shaped relationship between human-likeness of social media accounts and opinion polarization in replies mediated by their social validation and moderated by information valence. Originality/value Our findings advance understanding of human–bot interaction dynamics, highlighting how bot human-likeness relates to opinion polarization at the community level. This study provides actionable measures for stakeholders: bot developers should carefully calibrate human-likeness, platforms should implement graded indicators on human-likeness of social media accounts and users must critically evaluate information sources to mitigate polarization.

title: Water resilience in the high Andean basins of Peru and Ecuador: A synthesis of hydrological modeling, cryosphere dynamics, and ecohydrological approaches under climate change (2011–2025)
abstract: The high Andean basins of Peru and Ecuador supply freshwater to approximately 60% and 70% of their respective national populations. However, these systems are increasingly threatened by glacier retreat, land-use transformation, and climate variability, which jeopardize long-term water security. This study presents an integrative narrative review of 58 peer-reviewed scientific publications published between 2011 and 2025, focusing on hydrological modeling, cryospheric dynamics, hydrometeorological monitoring, climate change impacts, and ecohydrological processes in tropical Andean mountain systems. Following a systematic selection process, the reviewed evidence was organized into five thematic areas: advances in hydrological modeling under data-scarce conditions, validation of satellite precipitation products, glacio-hydrological and cryospheric dynamics, hydroclimatic scenario simulation, and ecohydrological approaches. The results reveal a sustained methodological transition from semi-distributed conceptual models (SWAT, HEC-HMS, and GR2M) toward physically based distributed models (MGB, PREVAH, and JULES), integrated with satellite products (GPM-IMERG, SM2RAIN, and ERA5-Land) and machine learning algorithms, significantly reducing the limitations associated with data scarcity. Climate projections under CMIP6 scenarios indicate increases of up to 60% in extreme precipitation intensity and up to 39% in annual runoff in some basins, while glacier mass loss could reduce dry-season water storage by as much as 25% over the coming decades. At the same time, land-use changes, including the conversion of páramo ecosystems to pasturelands and deforestation, have been shown to alter baseflow and infiltration processes independently of climatic forcing. The synthesis further reveals that water resilience in the Andes cannot be fully understood through physical hydrology alone. The conservation of water-regulating ecosystems such as páramos, bofedales, and montane forests plays a critical role in maintaining hydrological regulation and sustaining water availability under changing environmental conditions. The review highlights the importance of integrating hydrological processes, cryospheric dynamics, and ecosystem functions to improve water resilience assessments and support sustainable water resources management in the tropical Andes.

title: Walk the talk: how procurement professionals' interpretations shape social sustainability cascading
journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management
abstract: Purpose Procurement professionals shape how firms translate their commitments to social sustainability into supplier-facing governance, which can vary markedly, even within the same firm. This study explains this variation by theorizing how procurement professionals interpret their role and translate engagement with suppliers into governance practices. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on constructivist grounded theory and interviews with 27 professionals across organizational contexts. The analysis combines iterative coding, constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and abductive engagement with sensitizing literature. Findings The study develops a process model that explains cascading depth from a people-centric perspective. The interviewed procurement professionals differed on whether they construed their remit to include social sustainability, whether supplier-facing action appeared worth pursuing, and whether more improvement-oriented engagement appeared feasible. This situated judgment shaped whether cascading is enacted predominantly through procedural compliance or through more generative supplier-facing practice. Prospective paradoxical sensemaking helped explain how more generative supplier-facing responses could remain actionable under competing commercial demands, as professionals saw anticipated social and commercial consequences as relevant to their judgment in the present. Originality/value The study reframes cascading depth as a matter of how procurement professionals enact governance mechanisms. It specifies interpretive and relational conditions that remain underexplored in the literature on sustainable behavioral supply chain management. It extends paradoxical sensemaking research on how tensions are framed to include how more generative responses may be established and sustained in practice.

title: Validating and configuring a higher-order environmental ergonomics construct for occupant performance
abstract: Purpose This study empirically examines the influence of environmental ergonomics implementation (EEI) on indoor environmental comfort (IECP), cognitive and behavioral performance (CBP), health and wellbeing (HWP) and occupant productivity (OPP). By conceptualizing EEI as a multidimensional higher-order construct, the study assesses the strength of these relationships, identifies the most influential dimensions and explores how contextual combinations shape human-centered performance outcomes in real-world building environments. Design/methodology/approach A structured quantitative survey was administered to 106 built-environment professionals practicing in Lagos State, Nigeria. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to validate the higher-order EEI construct and estimate its predictive effects on the four outcome variables. To complement the net-effects analysis, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) was applied to identify configurational pathways, revealing how different combinations of EEI dimensions jointly lead to high levels of occupant performance. Findings The PLS-SEM results indicate that EEI has significant positive effects on all four human-centered performance dimensions, with the strongest effect observed for indoor environmental comfort. The fsQCA findings reveal multiple causal configurations through which EEI dimensions interact to produce optimal performance outcomes, highlighting the synergistic and multi-causal nature of environmental ergonomics in building contexts. Practical implications The findings underscore the need for stronger regulatory frameworks, targeted professional training, and sustained investment in ergonomics-enhancing technologies to improve human-centered building performance. Originality/value This study is among the first in the region to conceptualize and empirically validate environmental ergonomics implementation as a multidimensional higher-order construct and to examine its simultaneous effects on comfort, cognition, health and productivity using a combined PLS-SEM and fsQCA approach. It advances environmental ergonomics research by moving beyond isolated factor analysis toward an integrated, predictive and implementation-oriented perspective.

The effects of work overload on emotional exhaustion among nurses: serial mediation of job stress and depression
journal: Journal of Health Organization and Management
abstract: Purpose This study examines the relationship between work overload and emotional exhaustion among nurses. Specifically, the study investigates the serial mediating effect of job stress and depression on the relationship between work overload and emotional exhaustion. Design/methodology/approach Data were gathered between October 2025 and January 2026 through an online and face-to-face cross-sectional survey of 613 nurses working in two state hospitals in Türkiye. Sequential mediating effects were analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences PROCESS macro (Model 6). Findings The findings showed that work overload is positively related to emotional exhaustion. Furthermore, the results revealed that job stress and depression sequentially mediate the relationship between work overload and emotional exhaustion. Originality/value This research offers a clearer understanding of the potential psychological mechanisms underlying the relationship between work overload and emotional exhaustion among nurses. It also extends the literature by informing the development of interventions aimed at alleviating job stress and reducing depression levels among nurses in the healthcare sector. In particular, primary caregivers and hospital administrations responsible for nurses should develop work overload-conscious, stress-reducing, and mental health-supporting methods to improve nurse well-being and enhance the quality and safety of patient care.

title: Storage Virtualization for Hybrid Cloud: A Policy-Driven Object Storage Layer with Placement, Compliance, and Cost Constraints
journal: International Journal of Sustainability and Innovation in Engineering
abstract: The study proposes a policy-based S3-compatible virtualization layer that can be extended to both private MinIO/Ceph and public object storage services. It also analyzes five representative traces (T15, T29, T65, T78, and T79), containing about 17.4 million requests, within a larger set of about 1.6 billion requests that represent 342 million unique objects from a collection of traced IBM Cloud Object Storage requests. The 5 reported modeled-cost comparisons have a low of 38.7% modeled cost reduction compared to static tiering, a high of 47.2%, and an unweighted mean of 43.7%. These numbers refer to differences in the modeled totals, and do not represent statistically significant differences or newly confirmed cloud bills. Geography or regulatory classifications are not recorded with the dataset, and assumptions about compliance and causation of egress are made during simulation but not included in the dataset. HMAC-SHA-256 is used to validate the authenticity of policy metadata, rather than physical residence. Allows for repeatable assessments such as measurable tariff snapshots, baseline definition, fault-injection tests, and more.
